infectiousAgentClass: An InfectiousDisease is caused by an infectious agent class, which is an InfectiousAgentClass, categorizing the type of pathogen (e.g., bacteria, prion). Also called "pathogen class", "agent category", "type of infectious agent". Examples: "The disease is caused by an infectiousAgentClass 'Bacteria'.", "Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is caused by an infectiousAgentClass 'Prion'.", "COVID-19 is caused by an infectiousAgentClass 'Virus'."
ingredients: A Recipe includes ingredients, which are Text descriptions of single components used in the recipe. Also called "recipe components", "food items", "cooking elements". Examples: "The Recipe lists 'sugar' as an ingredient.", "The Recipe requires 'flour' as an ingredient.", "The Recipe includes 'garlic' as an ingredient."
inker: A ComicIssue, ComicStory, or VisualArtwork has an inker, who is a Person responsible for tracing over pencil drawings in ink. Also called "ink artist", "finisher (comics)", "ink illustrator". Examples: "The ComicIssue credits John Doe as the inker.", "The VisualArtwork has an inker Jane Smith.", "The ComicStory's inker completed the final lines."
insertion: A Muscle has an insertion, which is an AnatomicalStructure, representing the place of attachment of the muscle or what it moves. Also called "muscle attachment point", "distal attachment", "point of action". Examples: "The biceps muscle has an insertion on the radius bone.", "The deltoid muscle's insertion is on the humerus.", "The muscle's insertion allows it to move the limb."
installUrl: A SoftwareApplication has an install URL, which is a URL where the application may be installed, if different from its main URL. Also called "download link", "installation address", "setup URL". Examples: "The SoftwareApplication has an installUrl 'http://example.com/app/download'.", "The game's installUrl is on the platform's store.", "The SoftwareApplication provides an installUrl for direct download."
instructor: A CourseInstance has an instructor, who is a Person assigned to teach or provide instructional assistance for that course. Also called "taught by", "led by", "lectured by", "guided by". Examples: "The 'Introduction to Python' CourseInstance has an instructor named Dr. Smith.", "This yoga class CourseInstance has an instructor named Jane Doe.", "The 'Advanced Calculus' CourseInstance has an instructor who is a renowned professor."
instrument: An Action uses an instrument, which is a Thing that helped the agent perform the action. Also called "tool used", "means of action", "device employed". Examples: "John wrote a book with an instrument that was a pen.", "She cut the paper with an instrument that was scissors.", "The surgeon performed the operation with an instrument that was a scalpel."
intensity: An ExercisePlan has an intensity, which is a QuantitativeValue or Text, measuring the degree of force or velocity involved in the exercise. Also called "exercise effort", "workout level", "exertion rate". Examples: "The ExercisePlan specifies an intensity of '150 heartbeats per minute'.", "The workout has an intensity of 'moderate'.", "The ExercisePlan's intensity is described as 'high-impact'."
interactingDrug: A Drug interacts with another interacting drug, which is a Drug known to impact its effect or cause a risk to the patient. Also called "drug interaction", "concurrent medication", "co-administered drug". Examples: "Drug A has an interactingDrug, Drug B, which can reduce its effectiveness.", "This medication has an interactingDrug that increases side effects.", "The doctor checked for interactingDrugs before prescribing."
interactionCount: This property is deprecated, alongside the UserInteraction types on which it depended.
interactionService: An InteractionCounter uses an interaction service, which is a SoftwareApplication or WebSite where the interactions took place. Also called "platform of interaction", "service host", "interaction source". Examples: "The InteractionCounter recorded activity on the interactionService 'Facebook'.", "The InteractionCounter uses the interactionService 'Twitter'.", "The InteractionCounter tracks engagement on a specific WebSite."
interactionStatistic: A CreativeWork, Organization, or Person has an interaction statistic, which is an InteractionCounter, representing the number of interactions using a specific WebSite or SoftwareApplication. Also called "engagement metrics", "user activity count", "interaction tally". Examples: "The CreativeWork has an interactionStatistic showing 100 likes.", "The Organization's interactionStatistic indicates high user engagement.", "The Person's profile has an interactionStatistic for comments."
interactionType: An InteractionCounter represents an interaction type, which is an Action, specifying the kind of interaction (e.g., LikeAction, DislikeAction). Also called "type of engagement", "action category", "user action". Examples: "The InteractionCounter tracks an interactionType of 'LikeAction'.", "The statistic measures an interactionType of 'CommentAction'.", "The InteractionCounter records an interactionType that is a 'ShareAction'."
interactivityType: A CreativeWork has an interactivity type, which is Text, describing the predominant mode of learning supported by the resource (e.g., 'active', 'expositive', 'mixed'). Also called "learning mode", "engagement style", "pedagogical approach". Examples: "The CreativeWork has an interactivityType of 'active'.", "The video lecture has an interactivityType of 'expositive'.", "The online course's interactivityType is 'mixed'."
interestRate: A FinancialProduct has an interest rate, which is a Number or QuantitativeValue, representing the rate charged or paid. Also called "rate of interest", "borrowing cost", "yield rate". Examples: "The loan has an interestRate of 5%.", "The savings account offers an interestRate of 1.5%.", "The bond's interestRate is 3.25%."
interpretedAsClaim: A CreativeWork or MediaObject is interpreted as a claim, which is a Claim, indicating a specific assertion contained, implied, or derived from its content. Also called "contains claim", "implies assertion", "expresses claim". Examples: "The news article is interpretedAsClaim that 'the economy is improving'.", "The image is interpretedAsClaim that 'the event occurred'.", "The report is interpretedAsClaim that 'the product is safe'."

Also called "version date", "as-of date", "snapshot date". Examples: "Tax Law 2015 legislationDateVersion 2016-04-07", "Environmental Act legislationDateVersion 2023-03-01", "Labor Code legislationDateVersion 2022-10-15".
legislationEnsuresImplementationOf: This property indicates that a subject legislation ensures the implementation of an object legislation, often by modifying other laws to align with it. Also called "implements legislation", "enforces legislation", "gives effect to legislation". Examples: "National Law A legislationEnsuresImplementationOf EU Regulation B", "State Act X legislationEnsuresImplementationOf Federal Law Y", "Local Ordinance Z legislationEnsuresImplementationOf Regional Directive W". Distinct from legislationTransposes, which captures the transposition of directives.
legislationIdentifier: This property provides a unique identifier for a subject legislation, which can be a string-based code or a web-based URL/URI. Also called "legislation ID", "legal identifier", "official code". Examples: "EU Regulation 2016/679 legislationIdentifier CELEX:32016R0679", "French Law 2000-321 legislationIdentifier NOR:ECOX0000000L", "UK Act 2010 legislationIdentifier ELI/2010/ACT/123".
legislationJurisdiction: This property specifies the administrative area or legal authority from which a subject legislation originates. Also called "originating jurisdiction", "legal authority", "governing jurisdiction". Examples: "Federal Law legislationJurisdiction United States", "State Statute legislationJurisdiction California", "EU Directive legislationJurisdiction European Union".
legislationLegalForce: This property indicates the current legal status of a subject legislation, specifying if it is in force, not in force, or partially in force. Also called "legal status", "force status", "enforcement status". Examples: "Act A legislationLegalForce InForce", "Regulation B legislationLegalForce NotInForce", "Directive C legislationLegalForce PartiallyInForce". Distinct from legislationDateOfApplicability, which specifies when the legislation becomes applicable.
legislationLegalValue: This property describes the legal value level of a specific legislation file, acknowledging that different formats of the same legislation may hold varying legal weight. Also called "legal validity", "legal authority level", "official value". Examples: "Signed PDF legislationLegalValue StrongLegalValue", "HTML version legislationLegalValue WeakLegalValue", "Draft document legislationLegalValue NoLegalValue".
legislationPassedBy: This property identifies the organization or person that legally enacted or passed a subject legislation, serving as its legal author. Also called "enacted by", "promulgated by", "authorized by". Examples: "Act of Parliament legislationPassedBy The Parliament", "Government Decree legislationPassedBy The Cabinet", "Local Bylaw legislationPassedBy City Council". Distinct from legislationResponsible, which indicates the ministry or individual responsible for elaboration or questions.
legislationRepeals: This property indicates that a subject legislation repeals, cancels, or abrogates an object legislation. Also called "cancels legislation", "abrogates legislation", "overturns legislation". Examples: "New Act legislationRepeals Old Statute", "Regulation X legislationRepeals Directive Y", "Law Z legislationRepeals Previous Decree".
legislationResponsible: This property identifies the individual or organization responsible for a subject legislation, typically involved in its elaboration or as a point of contact for inquiries. Also called "responsible for legislation", "managed by", "oversight by". Examples: "Environmental Act legislationResponsible Ministry of Environment", "Tax Reform Bill legislationResponsible Department of Treasury", "Health Care Law legislationResponsible Ministry of Health". Distinct from legislationPassedBy, which identifies the legal author who enacted the law.
legislationTransposes: This property indicates that a subject legislation fulfills the objectives of an object legislation by implementing its measures, often creating a legally binding link. Also called "transposes directive", "implements directive", "incorporates legislation". Examples: "National Law A legislationTransposes EU Directive B", "Regional Act X legislationTransposes Federal Regulation Y", "Member State Law legislationTransposes European Directive". Distinct from legislationEnsuresImplementationOf, which broadly ensures implementation without the specific 'transposition' meaning.
legislationType: This property specifies the classification or type of a subject legislation, such as a law, act, directive, or regulation. Also called "kind of legislation", "legal instrument type", "form of law". Examples: "GDPR legislationType Regulation", "Copyright Act legislationType Law", "EU Directive 2006/123/EC legislationType Directive".
leiCode: This property provides a Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) code that uniquely identifies a subject organization according to ISO 17442. Also called "LEI identifier", "legal entity ID", "ISO 17442 identifier". Examples: "Company X leiCode 549300A1234567890A12", "Bank Y leiCode 254900O4L4L4L4L4L4L4", "Fund Z leiCode 987600ABCDEF12345678".
lender: This property identifies the organization or person who provides the object being borrowed in a subject BorrowAction. Also called "loan provider", "creditor", "giver of loan". Examples: "BorrowAction for car lender Bank of America", "BorrowAction for book lender Public Library", "BorrowAction for money lender John Doe".
lesser: This property indicates that a subject qualitative value is considered lesser than an object qualitative value in an ordered comparison. Also called "is less than", "is inferior to", "is smaller than". Examples: "Small lesser Medium", "Low lesser Moderate", "Cold lesser Warm". Distinct from lesserOrEqual, which includes equality in the comparison.
lesserOrEqual: This property indicates that a subject qualitative value is considered lesser than or equal to an object qualitative value in an ordered comparison. Also called "is less than or equal to", "is at most", "is no more than". Examples: "Small lesserOrEqual Medium", "Moderate lesserOrEqual Moderate", "Low lesserOrEqual High". Distinct from lesser, which strictly indicates inferiority without equality.
letterer: This property identifies the person who adds lettering, such as speech balloons and sound effects, to a subject comic issue, comic story, or visual artwork. Also called "lettered by", "text artist", "typographer". Examples: "Comic Book #1 letterer John Workman", "Graphic Novel X letterer Todd Klein", "Manga Series Y letterer Saori".
license: This property specifies the license document, often provided as a URL, that governs the usage and distribution of a subject creative work. Also called "under license", "licensed under", "usage terms". Examples: "Photo A license Creative Commons BY 4.0", "Software B license MIT License", "Article C license https://example.com/license.pdf".
lifeEvent: This property describes a significant event in a subject person's life, such as a baptism, communion, or burial. Also called "milestone event", "personal event", "biographical event". Examples: "John Doe lifeEvent His Wedding", "Jane Smith lifeEvent Her Graduation", "Baby Alex lifeEvent His Baptism".
line: This property defines a line within a subject GeoShape as a series of two or more point objects, representing a point-to-point path. Also called "path coordinates", "polyline", "geometric line". Examples: "Road Segment line '34.05,-118.25 34.06,-118.26'", "River Path line '40.71,-74.00 40.72,-74.01 40.73,-74.02'", "Border line '50.00,0.00 51.00,1.00'".
linkRelationship: This property specifies the type of relationship that a subject LinkRole represents for a web link. Also called "link type", "relationship type", "hyperlink relation". Examples: "LinkRole for 'next' linkRelationship 'next'", "LinkRole for 'author' linkRelationship 'author'", "LinkRole for 'stylesheet' linkRelationship 'stylesheet'".
liveBlogUpdate: This property indicates that an object BlogPosting serves as an update to a subject LiveBlogPosting. Also called "blog update", "live update", "new entry". Examples: "LiveBlog for Event A liveBlogUpdate 'New photo added'", "LiveBlog for Game B liveBlogUpdate 'Score update'", "LiveBlog for Conference C liveBlogUpdate 'Keynote speaker announced'".
loanMortgageMandateAmount: This property specifies the monetary amount of a mortgage mandate associated with a subject MortgageLoan, which can be converted into a full mortgage later. Also called "mandate amount", "potential mortgage amount", "pre-approved mortgage amount". Examples: "MortgageLoan A loanMortgageMandateAmount $200,000", "MortgageLoan B loanMortgageMandateAmount €350,000", "MortgageLoan C loanMortgageMandateAmount £150,000".
loanPaymentAmount: This property specifies the monetary amount required for a single payment within a subject RepaymentSpecification. Also called "payment amount", "installment amount", "due amount". Examples: "Loan Repayment Plan A loanPaymentAmount $500", "Mortgage Repayment Schedule B loanPaymentAmount €1200", "Credit Card Repayment C loanPaymentAmount £75".
loanPaymentFrequency: This property indicates the frequency of payments due for a subject RepaymentSpecification, expressed as the number of months between each payment. Also called "payment interval", "repayment frequency", "billing cycle". Examples: "Loan Repayment Plan A loanPaymentFrequency 1 (monthly)", "Mortgage Repayment Schedule B loanPaymentFrequency 3 (quarterly)", "Credit Repayment C loanPaymentFrequency 6 (semi-annually)".
loanRepaymentForm: This property describes the specific RepaymentSpecification for how money borrowed under a subject LoanOrCredit will be paid back to the lender. Also called "repayment method", "payment plan", "amortization schedule". Examples: "Car Loan loanRepaymentForm 'Monthly Installments'", "Student Credit loanRepaymentForm 'Income-Driven Repayment'", "Mortgage loanRepaymentForm 'Fixed-Rate Amortization'".
loanTerm: This property specifies the total duration or term of a subject loan or credit agreement. Also called "loan duration", "credit term", "repayment period". Examples: "Car Loan loanTerm '60 months'", "Mortgage loanTerm '30 years'", "Personal Loan loanTerm '5 years'".
loanType: This property specifies the category or type of a subject loan or credit, such as a mortgage or personal loan. Also called "credit type", "loan category", "financing type". Examples: "Home Loan loanType 'MortgageLoan'", "Student Loan loanType 'Federal Student Loan'", "Business Credit loanType 'Line of Credit'".
location: This property indicates the physical or virtual place where a subject action, event, interaction counter, or organization is situated or occurs. Also called "venue", "address", "site". Examples: "Concert Event location 'Madison Square Garden'", "Company Headquarters location '123 Main St, Anytown'", "Online Meeting location 'Zoom Link'". Distinct from locationCreated, which specifies where a creative work was originally made.
locationCreated: This property specifies the geographical place where a subject creative work was originally created or produced. Also called "place of creation", "origin location", "production site". Examples: "Painting 'Starry Night' locationCreated 'Saint-Rémy-de-Provence'", "Novel '1984' locationCreated 'London'", "Film 'Casablanca' locationCreated 'Hollywood'". Distinct from location, which indicates the current or primary location of an entity or event.
lodgingUnitDescription: This property provides a comprehensive textual description of the specific lodging unit reserved in a subject LodgingReservation. Also called "room description", "unit details", "accommodation features". Examples: "Hotel Reservation lodgingUnitDescription 'King-size bed, ocean view, private balcony'", "Cabin Booking lodgingUnitDescription 'Two bedrooms, fireplace, lake access'", "Apartment Rental lodgingUnitDescription 'Studio, kitchenette, city view'".
lodgingUnitType: This property specifies the type of lodging unit reserved in a subject LodgingReservation, including details like room vs. suite and bed size. Also called "room type", "accommodation type", "unit category". Examples: "Hotel Reservation lodgingUnitType 'Deluxe King Room'", "Resort Booking lodgingUnitType 'Family Suite'", "Hostel Reservation lodgingUnitType 'Shared Dormitory Bed'".
logo: This property provides an image object or URL representing the official logo associated with a subject brand, certification, organization, place, product, or service. Also called "brand emblem", "official symbol", "company logo". Examples: "Apple Inc. logo 'https://example.com/apple-logo.png'", "Product X logo 'imageobject:productX_logo'", "Certification Y logo 'https://example.com/cert-logo.svg'".
longitude: This property specifies the longitude coordinate of a subject geographical location or place, typically in WGS 84 format. Also called "longitudinal coordinate", "east-west position", "meridian value". Examples: "Eiffel Tower longitude 2.2945", "Statue of Liberty longitude -74.0445", "Mount Everest longitude 86.9250". Distinct from latitude, which specifies the north-south position.
loser: This property identifies the person who was defeated or lost in a subject WinAction. Also called "defeated participant", "vanquished", "opponent who lost". Examples: "Chess Match WinAction loser Garry Kasparov", "Debate WinAction loser Opponent Team", "Race WinAction loser Second Place Runner". Distinct from winner, which identifies the person who won the action.
lowPrice: This property specifies the lowest price among all available offers within a subject AggregateOffer. Also called "minimum price", "cheapest price", "starting price". Examples: "Product X AggregateOffer lowPrice 9.99", "Service Y AggregateOffer lowPrice 50.00", "Event Ticket AggregateOffer lowPrice 25.50". Distinct from highPrice, which specifies the highest price among available offers.
lyricist: This property identifies the person who wrote the words or lyrics for a subject MusicComposition. Also called "words by", "songwriter (lyrics)", "librettist". Examples: "Song A lyricist Bernie Taupin", "Musical B lyricist Tim Rice", "Opera C lyricist Lorenzo Da Ponte". Distinct from composer, who writes the music.
lyrics: This property provides the creative work containing the words or lyrics of a subject MusicComposition. Also called "song text", "words of song", "vocal text". Examples: "Song A lyrics 'CreativeWork of lyrics for Song A'", "Anthem B lyrics 'Text of Anthem B'", "Ballad C lyrics 'Poem for Ballad C'".
mainContentOfPage: This property indicates that an object WebPageElement constitutes the primary subject or main content of a subject WebPage. Also called "primary content", "main section", "central element". Examples: "Article Page mainContentOfPage 'Article Body Element'", "Product Page mainContentOfPage 'Product Description Section'", "Blog Post Page mainContentOfPage 'Blog Post Content'". Distinct from mainEntityOfPage, which indicates the main entity described by the page.
mainEntity: This property identifies the primary entity that is the central subject described within a subject creative work, such as a web page. Also called "primary subject", "about entity", "central topic". Examples: "Article about Eiffel Tower mainEntity Eiffel Tower", "Book about World War II mainEntity World War II", "Webpage about a product mainEntity The Product". Distinct from mainEntityOfPage, which links a Thing to the page describing it.
mainEntityOfPage: This property indicates the creative work or URL of a page for which a subject thing is the primary entity being described. Also called "described on page", "page's main subject", "primary page for". Examples: "Eiffel Tower mainEntityOfPage 'https://example.com/eiffel-tower'", "Product X mainEntityOfPage 'Product Page URL'", "Person Y mainEntityOfPage 'Biography WebPage'". Distinct from mainEntity, which links a CreativeWork to its main subject.
maintainer: This property identifies the person or organization responsible for managing contributions to and/or publication of a subject creative work, such as a dataset or software package. Also called "managed by", "curated by", "supported by". Examples: "Software Package A maintainer 'Open Source Community'", "Dataset B maintainer 'University Research Group'", "Project C maintainer 'John Doe'".
makesOffer: This property links a subject organization or person to an offer for products or services that they provide. Also called "offers", "provides offer", "sells". Examples: "Retailer X makesOffer 'Discounted Laptop Offer'", "Consultant Y makesOffer 'Hourly Service Offer'", "Restaurant Z makesOffer 'Dinner Menu Offer'".
manufacturer: This property identifies the organization responsible for manufacturing a subject product. Also called "made by", "produced by", "creator of product". Examples: "Smartphone X manufacturer 'TechCorp'", "Car Y manufacturer 'AutoMakers Inc.'", "Book Z manufacturer 'PrintHouse Ltd.'". Distinct from brand, which is the name under which a product is sold.
map: This property provides a URL linking to a map that depicts a subject place. Also called "map URL", "location map", "geographic map". Examples: "Restaurant A map 'https://maps.google.com/restaurantA'", "Park B map 'https://openstreetmap.org/parkB'", "Museum C map 'https://bing.com/maps/museumC'". Distinct from maps, which is a plural form and often used interchangeably but 'map' implies a single map.
mapType: This property specifies the category or kind of a subject map, chosen from the MapCategoryType enumeration. Also called "map category", "type of map", "map classification". Examples: "City Map mapType 'TransitMap'", "Hiking Map mapType 'TopographicMap'", "Road Map mapType 'RoadMap'".
maps: This property provides a URL linking to a map that depicts a subject place. Also called "map URL", "location map", "geographic map". Examples: "Restaurant A maps 'https://maps.google.com/restaurantA'", "Park B maps 'https://openstreetmap.org/parkB'", "Museum C maps 'https://bing.com/maps/museumC'". Distinct from map, which is a singular form and often used interchangeably but 'maps' implies multiple maps or a general reference.
marginOfError: This property specifies the quantitative value representing the margin of error associated with a subject observation. Also called "error margin", "measurement uncertainty", "tolerance range". Examples: "Poll Result Observation marginOfError '±3%'", "Experiment Measurement marginOfError '±0.5 units'", "Survey Data Observation marginOfError '±2.5 percentage points'".
masthead: This property provides a creative work or URL linking to the masthead page or a page listing top editorial management for a subject news media organization. Also called "editorial board", "management page", "staff directory". Examples: "Newspaper X masthead 'https://example.com/newspaperX/masthead'", "Online News Site Y masthead 'CreativeWork of Editorial Team'", "Magazine Z masthead 'https://example.com/magazineZ/about'".
material: This property specifies the material, as a product, text, or URL, from which a subject creative work or product is made. Also called "made of", "composed of", "fabric". Examples: "Jacket material 'Leather'", "Book material 'Paper'", "Sculpture material 'Bronze'".
materialExtent: This property describes the quantity of materials or the physical space occupied by them within a subject creative work. Also called "material quantity", "physical extent", "volume of material". Examples: "Sculpture materialExtent '50 kg of marble'", "Painting materialExtent '1 liter of oil paint'", "Building materialExtent '100 cubic meters of concrete'".
mathExpression: This property provides a mathematical expression, in various formats like LaTeX or plain text, that a subject MathSolver can process for solving, simplifying, or transforming. Also called "mathematical formula", "equation to solve", "algebraic expression". Examples: "MathSolver A mathExpression 'x^2 - 3x = 0'", "MathSolver B mathExpression '$\int x^2 dx$'", "MathSolver C mathExpression '2+2'".
maxPrice: This property specifies the highest numerical price within a range defined by a subject PriceSpecification. Also called "maximum price", "upper price limit", "highest cost". Examples: "Product PriceSpecification maxPrice 100.00", "Service PriceSpecification maxPrice 500.00", "Ticket PriceSpecification maxPrice 75.00". Distinct from minPrice, which specifies the lowest price in a range.
maxValue: This property specifies the upper numerical limit or maximum value for a subject monetary amount, property value, property value specification, or quantitative value. Also called "maximum limit", "upper bound", "highest value". Examples: "Temperature Range maxValue 30", "Age Limit maxValue 65", "Price Range maxValue 1000". Distinct from minValue, which specifies the lower value of a characteristic or property.
maximumAttendeeCapacity: This property specifies the total integer number of individuals who can attend a subject event or occupy a venue. Also called "total capacity", "attendee limit", "maximum occupancy". Examples: "Concert Event maximumAttendeeCapacity 10000", "Conference Venue maximumAttendeeCapacity 500", "Restaurant Place maximumAttendeeCapacity 80". Distinct from maximumPhysicalAttendeeCapacity, which specifies capacity for offline attendance.
maximumEnrollment: This property specifies the maximum integer number of students permitted to enroll in a subject educational or occupational program. Also called "enrollment limit", "student capacity", "maximum class size". Examples: "MBA Program maximumEnrollment 150", "Coding Bootcamp maximumEnrollment 30", "Online Course maximumEnrollment 500".
maximumIntake: This property specifies the recommended maximum intake of a subject dietary supplement, drug, drug strength, or substance for a particular population, as defined by a recommending authority. Also called "maximum dosage", "upper intake limit", "recommended max dose". Examples: "Vitamin C Supplement maximumIntake '2000 mg per day'", "Pain Reliever Drug maximumIntake '8 tablets in 24 hours'", "Substance X maximumIntake '100 micrograms'".
maximumPhysicalAttendeeCapacity: This property specifies the maximum integer capacity for physical attendees at a subject event, particularly for offline or mixed attendance modes. Also called "in-person capacity", "physical attendance limit", "venue capacity". Examples: "Conference Event maximumPhysicalAttendeeCapacity 500", "Concert Event maximumPhysicalAttendeeCapacity 10000", "Workshop Event maximumPhysicalAttendeeCapacity 50". Distinct from maximumVirtualAttendeeCapacity, which specifies capacity for online attendance.
maximumVirtualAttendeeCapacity: This property specifies the maximum integer capacity for virtual attendees at a subject event, particularly for online or mixed attendance modes. Also called "online capacity", "virtual attendance limit", "streaming capacity". Examples: "Webinar Event maximumVirtualAttendeeCapacity 1000", "Online Conference maximumVirtualAttendeeCapacity 5000", "Virtual Concert maximumVirtualAttendeeCapacity 100000". Distinct from maximumPhysicalAttendeeCapacity, which specifies capacity for offline attendance.
mealService: This property provides a textual description of the meal services, whether provided or available for purchase, on a subject flight. Also called "in-flight meals", "catering options", "food service". Examples: "Flight BA249 mealService 'Complimentary hot meal and beverages'", "Flight AA123 mealService 'Snacks and drinks available for purchase'", "Flight LH456 mealService 'Vegetarian and vegan options pre-orderable'".
measuredProperty: This property identifies the specific characteristic or property that is being measured or observed within a subject observation or statistical variable. Also called "property measured", "observed characteristic", "variable of interest". Examples: "Weather Observation measuredProperty 'Temperature'", "Survey Data measuredProperty 'Age'", "Medical Test measuredProperty 'Blood Pressure'". Distinct from measurementTechnique, which describes how the property was measured.
measurementDenominator: This property identifies the statistical variable that serves as the denominator when a subject observation or statistical variable represents a ratio or percentage. Also called "denominator variable", "ratio base", "reference variable". Examples: "Unemployment Rate Observation measurementDenominator 'Total Labor Force'", "Literacy Rate StatisticalVariable measurementDenominator 'Adult Population'", "Success Ratio Observation measurementDenominator 'Total Attempts'".
measurementMethod: This property specifies the particular method or technique used for measurement within a subject data catalog, dataset, observation, property value, or statistical variable. Also called "method of measurement", "data collection method", "analytical technique". Examples: "Dataset A measurementMethod 'Mass Spectrometry'", "Observation B measurementMethod 'Survey Questionnaire'", "StatisticalVariable C measurementMethod 'Census Data Collection'". Distinct from measurementTechnique, which is a broader property for the overall technique.
measurementQualifier: This property provides additional qualification or context to a subject observation or statistical variable, such as specifying if a value is nominal or real. Also called "measurement context", "qualifying factor", "data attribute". Examples: "GDP Observation measurementQualifier 'Nominal'", "Inflation Rate StatisticalVariable measurementQualifier 'Annualized'", "Temperature Reading measurementQualifier 'Average'".
measurementTechnique: This property describes the overall technique, method, or technology employed to measure variables within a subject data catalog, dataset, observation, property value, or statistical variable. Also called "measurement methodology", "data acquisition technique", "analytical approach". Examples: "Dataset A measurementTechnique 'NMR Spectroscopy'", "Observation B measurementTechnique 'Zung Scale'", "StatisticalVariable C measurementTechnique 'Satellite Imagery Analysis'". Distinct from measurementMethod, which is a subproperty for specifying more specific methods.
mechanismOfAction: This property describes the specific biochemical interaction by which a subject dietary supplement or drug produces its pharmacological effect. Also called "mode of action", "pharmacological mechanism", "how it works". Examples: "Drug X mechanismOfAction 'Inhibits enzyme Y'", "Supplement Z mechanismOfAction 'Acts as antioxidant'", "Medication A mechanismOfAction 'Blocks receptor B'".
mediaAuthenticityCategory: This property assigns a MediaManipulationRatingEnumeration classification to a media object within a subject MediaReview, based on its authenticity and how it was published or shared. Also called "media authenticity rating", "manipulation classification", "content integrity category". Examples: "Image Review mediaAuthenticityCategory 'TransformedContent'", "Video Review mediaAuthenticityCategory 'OriginalContent'", "Audio Review mediaAuthenticityCategory 'EditedContent'".
mediaItemAppearance: This property indicates the specific media object(s) that are grouped together within a subject MediaReviewItem for review. Also called "reviewed media item", "media object in review", "item under scrutiny". Examples: "MediaReviewItem A mediaItemAppearance 'Image of politician'", "MediaReviewItem B mediaItemAppearance 'Video clip of speech'", "MediaReviewItem C mediaItemAppearance 'Audio recording'".
median: This property specifies the median numerical value within a subject quantitative value distribution. Also called "middle value", "50th percentile", "central tendency". Examples: "Income Distribution median 50000", "Test Score Distribution median 75", "Age Distribution median 35". Distinct from mean, which is the average value.
medicalAudience: This property specifies the intended medical audience or audience type for a subject medical web page. Also called "target medical audience", "intended readership", "audience type". Examples: "Research Article medicalAudience 'MedicalResearchers'", "Patient Information Page medicalAudience 'Patients'", "Clinical Guideline medicalAudience 'Physicians'".
medicalSpecialty: This property specifies the medical specialty practiced by a subject hospital, medical clinic, medical organization, or physician. Also called "specialization", "area of expertise", "clinical focus". Examples: "Dr. Smith medicalSpecialty 'Cardiology'", "Hospital X medicalSpecialty 'Pediatrics'", "Clinic Y medicalSpecialty 'Dermatology'".
medicineSystem: This property specifies the system of medicine, such as 'evidence-based' or 'homeopathic', to which a subject medical entity belongs. Also called "medical paradigm", "healthcare system", "treatment approach". Examples: "Drug A medicineSystem 'EvidenceBasedMedicine'", "Therapy B medicineSystem 'HomeopathicMedicine'", "Procedure C medicineSystem 'Chiropractic'".
meetsEmissionStandard: This property indicates that a subject vehicle complies with a specified emission standard, represented as a qualitative value, text, or URL. Also called "emission compliant", "emission certified", "environmental standard met". Examples: "Car X meetsEmissionStandard 'Euro 6'", "Truck Y meetsEmissionStandard 'CARB Compliant'", "Motorcycle Z meetsEmissionStandard 'https://example.com/emission-standard-A'".
member: This property identifies an organization or person who is a member of a subject organization or program membership. Also called "has member", "includes member", "comprises member". Examples: "Club A member 'John Doe'", "Company B member 'Subsidiary C'", "ProgramMembership X member 'Jane Smith'". Distinct from memberOf, which indicates the organization or program a person/organization belongs to.
memberOf: This property indicates the organization, program membership, or member program tier to which a subject person or organization belongs. Also called "belongs to", "is a member of", "affiliated with". Examples: "John Doe memberOf 'Sports Club'", "Company X memberOf 'Industry Association'", "Jane Smith memberOf 'Gold Tier Membership'". Distinct from member, which identifies members of an organization or program.
members: This property identifies an organization or person who is a member of a subject organization or program membership. Also called "has members", "includes members", "comprises members". Examples: "Club A members 'John Doe'", "Company B members 'Subsidiary C'", "ProgramMembership X members 'Jane Smith'". Distinct from memberOf, which indicates the organization or program a person/organization belongs to.
membershipNumber: This property provides a unique textual identifier for a subject program membership. Also called "member ID", "membership ID", "account number". Examples: "Loyalty Program Membership membershipNumber '123456789'", "Gym Membership membershipNumber 'G-98765'", "Club Membership membershipNumber 'ABC-001'".
membershipPointsEarned: This property specifies the number or quantitative value of membership points earned by a member within a subject member program tier, price specification, or program membership. Also called "points accumulated", "rewards points", "loyalty points". Examples: "Gold Tier Membership membershipPointsEarned 5000", "Flight Program Membership membershipPointsEarned '10000 miles'", "Retailer Program membershipPointsEarned 250 'stars'".
memoryRequirements: This property specifies the minimum memory requirements, as text or a URL, for a subject software application to function. Also called "RAM requirements", "memory needed", "system memory". Examples: "Software A memoryRequirements '8 GB RAM'", "Application B memoryRequirements 'https://example.com/specs#memory'", "Game C memoryRequirements '16 GB DDR4'".
mentions: This property indicates that a subject creative work includes a reference to an object thing, without necessarily being primarily about that thing. Also called "refers to", "cites", "references". Examples: "Article about climate change mentions 'Paris Agreement'", "Book about history mentions 'Napoleon Bonaparte'", "Report on economy mentions 'inflation'". Distinct from about, which indicates the primary topic of the creative work.
menu: This property provides the menu for a subject food establishment, which can be a structured representation, plain text, or a URL. Also called "food offerings", "dining options", "restaurant menu". Examples: "Restaurant A menu 'https://example.com/menu.pdf'", "Cafe B menu 'Coffee, Tea, Pastries'", "Diner C menu 'Menu object with sections'".
menuAddOn: This property specifies an additional menu item or a menu section of allowed add-ons that can be paired with a subject menu item. Also called "side order", "optional extra", "complementary item". Examples: "Burger MenuItem menuAddOn 'Fries'", "Steak MenuItem menuAddOn 'Side Salad'", "Pizza MenuItem menuAddOn 'Extra Toppings Section'".
merchant: This property identifies the organization or person acting as the seller for a subject order. Also called "seller", "vendor", "retailer". Examples: "Online Order merchant 'Amazon.com'", "Local Purchase merchant 'Corner Store'", "Service Booking merchant 'Service Provider Inc.'".
merchantReturnDays: This property specifies either a fixed return date or the number of days from delivery within which a product can be returned, applicable when the return policy is a finite window. Also called "return period", "days for return", "return window". Examples: "Return Policy A merchantReturnDays 30", "Seasonal Return Policy B merchantReturnDays '2024-01-31'", "Product Return Policy C merchantReturnDays 14".
merchantReturnLink: This property provides a URL to a web page or service dedicated to product returns, as part of a subject merchant return policy. Also called "return policy URL", "returns page", "customer returns link". Examples: "Return Policy A merchantReturnLink 'https://example.com/returns'", "Store Return Policy B merchantReturnLink 'https://shop.com/return-info'", "Online Retailer Policy C merchantReturnLink 'https://help.retailer.com/returns'".
messageAttachment: This property indicates a creative work that is attached to a subject message. Also called "attached file", "email attachment", "message content". Examples: "Email Message messageAttachment 'Document.pdf'", "Chat Message messageAttachment 'Image.jpg'", "Forum Post messageAttachment 'Spreadsheet.xlsx'".
mileageFromOdometer: This property specifies the total distance a subject vehicle has traveled since its production, as indicated by its odometer reading. Also called "odometer reading", "total mileage", "distance traveled". Examples: "Car A mileageFromOdometer '50000 KMT'", "Truck B mileageFromOdometer '120000 SMI'", "Motorcycle C mileageFromOdometer '15000 km'".
minPrice: This property specifies the lowest numerical price within a range defined by a subject PriceSpecification. Also called "minimum price", "lower price limit", "starting cost". Examples: "Product PriceSpecification minPrice 10.00", "Service PriceSpecification minPrice 50.00", "Ticket PriceSpecification minPrice 25.00". Distinct from maxPrice, which specifies the highest price in a range.
minValue: This property specifies the lower numerical limit or minimum value for a subject monetary amount, property value, property value specification, or quantitative value. Also called "minimum limit", "lower bound", "lowest value". Examples: "Temperature Range minValue 10", "Age Limit minValue 18", "Price Range minValue 100". Distinct from maxValue, which specifies the upper value of a characteristic or property.
minimumPaymentDue: This property specifies the minimum monetary amount or price specification that is currently required as payment for a subject invoice. Also called "minimum amount due", "lowest payment required", "current minimum payment". Examples: "Invoice A minimumPaymentDue '$50.00'", "Invoice B minimumPaymentDue 'PriceSpecification for $25.00'", "Invoice C minimumPaymentDue '$100.00'".
missionCoveragePrioritiesPolicy: This property provides a creative work or URL containing a statement from a subject news media organization regarding its coverage priorities, public agenda, or stance on issues. Also called "editorial policy", "coverage guidelines", "mission statement". Examples: "News Outlet A missionCoveragePrioritiesPolicy 'https://example.com/ethics'", "Journalism Group B missionCoveragePrioritiesPolicy 'Statement on impartiality'", "Media Company C missionCoveragePrioritiesPolicy 'https://example.com/mission'".
mobileUrl: This property provides a URL specifically for a dedicated mobile version of a subject offer or product page, distinct from its main URL. Also called "mobile site URL", "responsive URL", "mobile-friendly link". Examples: "Product A mobileUrl 'https://m.example.com/productA'", "Offer B mobileUrl 'https://mobile.shop.com/offerB'", "Product C mobileUrl 'https://example.com/mobile/itemC'". Distinct from url, which is the general URL for the page, ideally responsive.
model: This property specifies the model of a subject product, either as a ProductModel URL or a textual identifier. Also called "product model number", "version", "type". Examples: "Smartphone X model 'iPhone 15 Pro'", "Car Y model 'Model S'", "Laptop Z model 'ProductModel URL for XPS 15'". Distinct from brand, which is the name under which a product is sold.
modelDate: This property specifies the release date of a subject vehicle model, often used to distinguish different versions of the same make and model. Also called "model year", "release date", "version date". Examples: "Car Model A modelDate '2023-09-01'", "Motorcycle Model B modelDate '2024-01-15'", "Truck Model C modelDate '2022-07-01'".
modifiedTime: This property specifies the date and time when a subject reservation was last modified. Also called "last modified date", "update timestamp", "change date". Examples: "Flight Reservation modifiedTime '2023-10-26T10:30:00Z'", "Hotel Booking modifiedTime '2024-01-05T14:00:00Z'", "Restaurant Reservation modifiedTime '2023-11-20T18:15:00Z'". Distinct from bookingTime, which is when the reservation was originally made.
molecularFormula: This property provides the empirical molecular formula, representing the simplest whole number ratio of atoms, for a subject molecular entity. Also called "empirical formula", "chemical formula", "composition formula". Examples: "Water molecularFormula 'H2O'", "Glucose molecularFormula 'C6H12O6'", "Methane molecularFormula 'CH4'".
molecularWeight: This property specifies the molecular weight of a subject molecular entity, including its numerical value and units. Also called "molecular mass", "formula weight", "relative molecular mass". Examples: "Water molecularWeight '18.015 amu'", "Carbon Dioxide molecularWeight '44.01 g/mol'", "Compound X molecularWeight 'QuantitativeValue of 150.2 Da'".
monoisotopicMolecularWeight: A MolecularEntity has a monoisotopic molecular weight, which is the sum of the masses of its atoms using the most abundant isotope for each element. Also called has monoisotopic mass, is monoisotopic molecularly weighted at, monoisotopic mass of. Examples: Water has monoisotopic molecular weight '18.010565 g/mol'. Methane has monoisotopic molecular weight '16.031300 g/mol'. A protein has monoisotopic molecular weight '25000 g/mol'.
monthlyMinimumRepaymentAmount: A PaymentCard requires a monthly minimum repayment amount, which is the lowest sum of money due on a credit card statement each month. Also called has minimum monthly payment, requires minimum monthly repayment, minimum payment for. Examples: A credit card has monthly minimum repayment amount '$25'. A store card has monthly minimum repayment amount '2% of balance'. My Visa card has monthly minimum repayment amount '$50'.
monthsOfExperience: OccupationalExperienceRequirements specify the minimal number of months of experience required for a position. Also called requires months of experience, minimum experience in months, experience duration in months. Examples: Software Engineer requirements specify months of experience 36. Marketing Manager requirements specify months of experience 60. Entry-level position requirements specify months of experience 0.
mpn: A Demand, Offer, or Product has an MPN (Manufacturer Part Number), which is a unique identifier assigned by the manufacturer. Also called has manufacturer part number, product code, part number. Examples: A laptop has MPN 'XPS13-9310'. An offer refers to a product with MPN 'ABC-12345'. A demand is for a component with MPN 'XYZ-987'. Distinct from gtin, which is a globally unique trade item number.
multipleValues: A PropertyValueSpecification indicates whether multiple values are allowed for the property it describes. Also called allows multiple values, supports multiple entries, is multi-valued. Examples: A color property specification indicates multiple values true. A single-choice option specification indicates multiple values false. A tag property specification indicates multiple values true.
muscleAction: A Muscle generates a specific muscle action, which is the movement it produces. Also called performs action, causes movement, function of muscle. Examples: Biceps brachii has muscle action 'flexion of elbow'. Triceps brachii has muscle action 'extension of elbow'. Gastrocnemius has muscle action 'plantarflexion of foot'.
musicArrangement: A MusicComposition has a music arrangement, which is another musical composition derived from it. Also called has arrangement, is arranged as, version of composition. Examples: Beethoven's Symphony No. 5 has music arrangement 'Liszt's piano transcription'. A folk song has music arrangement 'jazz quartet version'. Bach's Cello Suite No. 1 has music arrangement 'guitar arrangement'.
musicBy: A Clip, Episode, Movie, or other video-related work features music by a specific MusicGroup or Person, who is the composer of its soundtrack. Also called soundtrack by, composed by, features music from. Examples: The movie 'Inception' has music by 'Hans Zimmer'. An episode of 'Game of Thrones' has music by 'Ramin Djawadi'. The video game 'Final Fantasy VII' has music by 'Nobuo Uematsu'. Distinct from composer, which is for the composer of a MusicComposition.
musicCompositionForm: A MusicComposition is characterized by its music composition form, which describes its type (e.g., overture, sonata, symphony). Also called composition type, form of music, genre of composition. Examples: Beethoven's Symphony No. 5 has music composition form 'Symphony'. Chopin's Piano Sonata No. 2 has music composition form 'Sonata'. Rossini's William Tell has music composition form 'Overture'.
musicGroupMember: A MusicGroup includes a music group member, who is an individual person belonging to that group. Also called member of group, band member, artist in group. Examples: The Beatles has music group member 'John Lennon'. Queen has music group member 'Freddie Mercury'. Fleetwood Mac has music group member 'Stevie Nicks'.
musicReleaseFormat: A MusicRelease is distributed in a specific music release format, indicating the type of recording media used. Also called release format, media type, recording format. Examples: An album release has music release format 'CompactDisc'. A single release has music release format 'DigitalAudio'. A classic rock album has music release format 'VinylFormat'.
musicalKey: A MusicComposition is written in a specific musical key, which defines its tonal center, mode, or scale. Also called key signature, key of composition, tonal key. Examples: Beethoven's Symphony No. 5 has musical key 'C minor'. A jazz standard has musical key 'Bb major'. A folk tune has musical key 'Dorian mode'.
naics: An Organization or Person is classified by a NAICS code, which is its North American Industry Classification System code. Also called NAICS classification, industry code, business classification. Examples: A software company has NAICS '511210'. A restaurant has NAICS '722511'. A freelance writer has NAICS '711510'. Distinct from isicV4, which is an international industry classification.
name: A Thing is identified by its name, which is a common textual label for it. Also called is called, title, label. Examples: A book has name 'The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy'. A person has name 'Alice Smith'. A company has name 'Acme Corp'. Distinct from alternateName, which is a secondary name.
namedPosition: A Role specifies a named position, which is the particular position played or filled by a person or organization within a larger organization. Also called role title, position held, job title. Examples: A player's role has named position 'Quarterback'. An employee's role has named position 'Senior Software Engineer'. A board member's role has named position 'Treasurer'. Distinct from roleName, which is a more general description of the role.
nationality: A Person holds a specific nationality, indicating the country of their citizenship or origin. Also called is a national of, citizenship, country of origin. Examples: John Doe has nationality 'United States'. Marie Curie had nationality 'Poland'. A traveler has nationality 'Germany'. Distinct from birthPlace, which is where the person was born.
naturalProgression: A MedicalCondition exhibits a natural progression, which describes its expected course if left untreated. Also called untreated course, disease progression, natural history. Examples: Common cold has natural progression 'resolves in 7-10 days'. Untreated diabetes has natural progression 'worsening symptoms and complications'. A minor cut has natural progression 'heals within a week'.
negativeNotes: A Product or Review includes negative notes, which are critical considerations or drawbacks regarding the item. Also called cons, disadvantages, drawbacks, criticisms. Examples: A phone review has negative notes 'short battery life'. A product description has negative notes 'high price'. A movie review has negative notes 'slow pacing'. Distinct from positiveNotes, which describes favorable aspects.
nerve: A Muscle is innervated by a specific nerve, which controls its function. Also called innervated by, supplied by nerve, controlled by nerve. Examples: Biceps brachii has nerve 'Musculocutaneous nerve'. Triceps brachii has nerve 'Radial nerve'. Diaphragm has nerve 'Phrenic nerve'. Distinct from nerveMotor, which describes the muscle controlled by a nerve.
nerveMotor: A Nerve provides motor control to a specific muscle, indicating the neurological pathway that activates it. Also called controls muscle, innervates muscle, motor innervation of. Examples: The Radial nerve has nerve motor 'Triceps brachii'. The Musculocutaneous nerve has nerve motor 'Biceps brachii'. The Phrenic nerve has nerve motor 'Diaphragm'. Distinct from nerve, which describes the nerve innervating a muscle.
netWorth: A Person possesses a net worth, which is their total financial value calculated by subtracting liabilities from assets. Also called total assets minus liabilities, financial value, wealth. Examples: A billionaire has net worth '$100 billion'. An individual has net worth '$500,000'. A recent graduate has net worth '$10,000'.
newsUpdatesAndGuidelines: A SpecialAnnouncement points to news updates and guidelines, which is a URL or WebContent page containing further information and directives. Also called related news page, guidance page, updates link. Examples: A COVID-19 announcement has news updates and guidelines 'https://example.com/covid-updates'. A storm warning has news updates and guidelines 'https://localweather.gov/storm-guidelines'. A product recall announcement has news updates and guidelines 'https://manufacturer.com/recall-info'.
nextItem: A ListItem is followed by a next item, which is the subsequent ListItem in an ordered sequence. Also called followed by, succeeding item, next in list. Examples: Item 1 has next item 'Item 2'. The second step has next item 'the third step'. A chapter in a book has next item 'the subsequent chapter'. Distinct from previousItem, which points to the preceding item.
noBylinesPolicy: A NewsMediaOrganization adheres to a no bylines policy, which is a statement explaining the circumstances under which authors of articles are not credited in bylines. Also called anonymous author policy, bylines exclusion policy, author attribution policy. Examples: A newspaper has no bylines policy 'https://example.com/anon-policy'. An investigative journalism organization has no bylines policy 'for sensitive reports'. A news agency has no bylines policy 'when sources require anonymity'.
nonEqual: A QualitativeValue is non-equal to another QualitativeValue, indicating that the subject value is distinct from the object value. Also called is not equal to, differs from, is unequal to. Examples: Good is non-equal 'Bad'. High is non-equal 'Low'. Red is non-equal 'Blue'. Distinct from equal, which indicates equivalence.
nonProprietaryName: A DietarySupplement or Drug has a non-proprietary name, which is its generic or common name, distinct from any brand name. Also called generic name, common name, chemical name. Examples: Tylenol has non-proprietary name 'Acetaminophen'. Advil has non-proprietary name 'Ibuprofen'. A vitamin C supplement has non-proprietary name 'Ascorbic Acid'. Distinct from brand, which is the proprietary name.
nonprofitStatus: An Organization holds a specific nonprofit status, which describes its legal classification as a non-profit entity in its primary business location. Also called non-profit classification, charity status, tax-exempt status. Examples: A charity organization has nonprofit status 'Nonprofit501c3'. A social club has nonprofit status 'Nonprofit501c7'. A research foundation has nonprofit status 'Nonprofit501c3'.
normalRange: A MedicalTest has a normal range, which specifies the acceptable values for a typical patient. Also called reference range, healthy range, typical values. Examples: A blood pressure test has normal range '120/80 mmHg'. A glucose test has normal range '70-99 mg/dL'. A cholesterol test has normal range 'below 200 mg/dL'.
nsn: A Product is identified by its NSN (NATO Stock Number), which is a 13-digit numeric code used in the NATO supply chain. Also called NATO stock number, military part number, supply code. Examples: A military vehicle part has NSN '2510-01-123-4567'. A defense supply item has NSN '4240-00-987-6543'. A specific tool has NSN '5120-01-000-1111'. Distinct from mpn, which is a manufacturer part number.
numAdults: A LodgingReservation specifies the num adults, which is the count of adult guests included in the reservation. Also called number of adult guests, adult count, adults booked. Examples: A hotel reservation has num adults 2. A cabin booking has num adults 4. A single room reservation has num adults 1. Distinct from numChildren, which specifies the count of child guests.
numChildren: A LodgingReservation specifies the num children, which is the count of child guests included in the reservation. Also called number of child guests, child count, children booked. Examples: A family hotel reservation has num children 2. A resort booking has num children 3. A room reservation has num children 0. Distinct from numAdults, which specifies the count of adult guests.
numConstraints: A ConstraintNode has num constraints, which indicates the total count of constraint property values defined for it. Also called constraint count, number of defined constraints, total constraints. Examples: A statistical variable has num constraints 5. A data model constraint node has num constraints 3. A query filter has num constraints 2.
numItems: ShippingConditions apply to a specific num items, which limits the quantity of items being shipped under these conditions. Also called item quantity limit, number of items covered, item count for shipping. Examples: Free shipping conditions apply to num items 'up to 5'. Express shipping conditions apply to num items '1-10'. Bulk discount conditions apply to num items '50 or more'. Distinct from numberOfItems (for ItemList), which is the total count of items in a list.
numTracks: A MusicPlaylist contains num tracks, which is the total count of individual musical tracks within it. Also called track count, number of songs, total tracks. Examples: An album has num tracks 12. A playlist has num tracks 25. A single has num tracks 1.
numberOfAccommodationUnits: An ApartmentComplex or FloorPlan has a number of accommodation units, representing the total count of all units, both available and unavailable. Also called total units, total accommodation count, unit capacity. Examples: An apartment complex has number of accommodation units 200. A floor plan has number of accommodation units 1. A building has number of accommodation units 50. Distinct from numberOfAvailableAccommodationUnits, which specifies only the currently available units.
numberOfAirbags: A Vehicle is equipped with a number of airbags, indicating the count or type of safety airbags present. Also called airbag count, airbag system, safety airbags. Examples: A car has number of airbags 6. A truck has number of airbags 'front and side'. A luxury sedan has number of airbags 8.
numberOfAvailableAccommodationUnits: An ApartmentComplex or FloorPlan has a number of available accommodation units, indicating the count of units currently ready for occupancy. Also called available units, vacant units, units for rent. Examples: An apartment complex has number of available accommodation units 15. A floor plan has number of available accommodation units 1. A hotel has number of available accommodation units 50. Distinct from numberOfAccommodationUnits, which specifies the total count of all units.
numberOfAxles: A Vehicle is built with a number of axles, which is the count of shafts connecting opposing wheels. Also called axle count, axles present, wheel axles. Examples: A standard car has number of axles 2. A semi-trailer truck has number of axles 5. A bus has number of axles 3.
numberOfBathroomsTotal: An Accommodation or FloorPlan has a number of bathrooms total, which is the sum of all full and partial bathrooms, following real estate conventions. Also called total bathroom count, total number of washrooms, bathroom sum. Examples: A house has number of bathrooms total 3. An apartment has number of bathrooms total 2. A studio has number of bathrooms total 1. Distinct from numberOfFullBathrooms and numberOfPartialBathrooms, which specify counts of specific bathroom types.
numberOfBedrooms: An Accommodation, ApartmentComplex, or FloorPlan has a number of bedrooms, indicating the total count of sleeping rooms. Also called bedroom count, total bedrooms, sleeping rooms. Examples: A house has number of bedrooms 3. An apartment complex offers units with number of bedrooms 2. A floor plan shows number of bedrooms 1. Distinct from numberOfBeds, which is the count of actual beds.
numberOfBeds: BedDetails specify the number of beds, which is the quantity of a particular bed type available in a lodging unit. Also called bed count, quantity of beds, beds available. Examples: A king bed room has number of beds 1. A twin room has number of beds 2. A family suite has number of beds 3. Distinct from numberOfBedrooms, which is the count of rooms designated for sleeping.
numberOfCredits: A Course or EducationalOccupationalProgram awards a number of credits, which is the quantity of academic or professional units earned upon completion. Also called credit count, units awarded, course credits. Examples: A university course has number of credits 3. A master's program has number of credits 30. A certification program has number of credits 10.
numberOfDoors: A Vehicle is equipped with a number of doors, indicating the total count of entry and exit points. Also called door count, total doors, vehicle doors. Examples: A sports car has number of doors 2. A family sedan has number of doors 4. A hatchback has number of doors 5.
numberOfEmployees: A BusinessAudience or Organization has a number of employees, which is the total count of individuals working for it. Also called employee count, staff size, workforce size. Examples: A small business has number of employees 15. A large corporation has number of employees 10,000. A startup has number of employees 5.
numberOfEpisodes: A CreativeWorkSeason, RadioSeries, TVSeries, or VideoGameSeries contains a number of episodes, which is the total count of individual installments within it. Also called episode count, total episodes, installments. Examples: Season 1 of a TV show has number of episodes 10. A radio series has number of episodes 52. A video game series has number of episodes 3. Distinct from numberOfSeasons, which is the count of seasons.
numberOfForwardGears: A Vehicle's transmission system has a number of forward gears, indicating the total count of gears available for moving forward. Also called forward gear count, transmission gears, gear ratio count. Examples: A manual car has number of forward gears 6. An automatic car has number of forward gears 8. A truck has number of forward gears 10.
numberOfFullBathrooms: An Accommodation or FloorPlan has a number of full bathrooms, which is the total count of full and three-quarter bathrooms. Also called full bathroom count, complete bathrooms, bathrooms with shower/tub. Examples: A house has number of full bathrooms 2. An apartment has number of full bathrooms 1. A luxury suite has number of full bathrooms 3. Distinct from numberOfPartialBathrooms, which counts half or quarter bathrooms.
numberOfItems: An ItemList contains a number of items, which is the total count of entries within the list. Also called item count, total items, list size. Examples: A shopping list has number of items 5. A playlist has number of items 20. A search results page has number of items 100. Distinct from numItems (for ShippingConditions), which limits the quantity for shipping.
numberOfLoanPayments: A RepaymentSpecification defines the number of loan payments, which is the total count of contractually required payments to repay a loan. Also called payment count, loan installments, repayment schedule length. Examples: A 30-year mortgage has number of loan payments 360. A car loan has number of loan payments 60. A short-term loan has number of loan payments 12.
numberOfPages: A Book consists of a number of pages, which is the total count of pages it contains. Also called page count, total pages, book length. Examples: A novel has number of pages 350. A textbook has number of pages 800. A children's book has number of pages 32.
numberOfPartialBathrooms: An Accommodation or FloorPlan has a number of partial bathrooms, which is the total count of half and quarter bathrooms. Also called half bathroom count, partial washrooms, guest toilets. Examples: A house has number of partial bathrooms 1. An apartment has number of partial bathrooms 0. A large office has number of partial bathrooms 4. Distinct from numberOfFullBathrooms, which counts full or three-quarter bathrooms.
numberOfPlayers: A Game or VideoGameSeries supports a number of players, indicating the minimum, maximum, or range of participants. Also called player count, player capacity, number of participants. Examples: A board game has number of players '2-4'. A video game has number of players '1'. An online game has number of players 'up to 64'.
numberOfPreviousOwners: A Vehicle has a number of previous owners, which is the total count of all owners, including the current one. Also called owner count, prior owners, ownership history length. Examples: A used car has number of previous owners 2. A classic car has number of previous owners 5. A new car has number of previous owners 1 (the current owner).
numberOfRooms: An Accommodation or LodgingBusiness has a number of rooms, which is the total count of rooms, excluding bathrooms and closets. Also called room count, total rooms, room quantity. Examples: A house has number of rooms 6. An apartment has number of rooms 3. A hotel suite has number of rooms 2. Distinct from numberOfBedrooms, which specifically counts sleeping rooms.
numberOfSeasons: A RadioSeries, TVSeries, or VideoGameSeries consists of a number of seasons, which is the total count of distinct seasons within the series. Also called season count, total seasons, series seasons. Examples: A TV series has number of seasons 8. A radio drama has number of seasons 3. A video game series has number of seasons 2. Distinct from numberOfEpisodes, which is the count of episodes within a season or series.
numberedPosition: An OrganizationRole is associated with a numbered position, which is a numerical identifier for that role within an organization. Also called role number, position number, jersey number. Examples: An athlete's role has numbered position 23. A team member's role has numbered position 7. A player's role has numbered position 10.
nutrition: A MenuItem or Recipe provides nutrition information, detailing its nutritional content. Also called nutritional facts, calorie count, dietary information. Examples: A salad recipe has nutrition '250 calories, 10g fat'. A menu item has nutrition '300 calories, 15g protein'. A smoothie recipe has nutrition '180 calories, 5g fiber'.
object: An Action is performed upon an object, which is the entity whose state is affected or remains intact by the action. Also called target of action, affected entity, patient. Examples: Reading action has object 'a book'. Eating action has object 'an apple'. Repairing action has object 'a car'. Distinct from agent, which is the performer of the action.
observationAbout: An Observation is about a specific place or thing, identifying the entity to which the observation pertains. Also called pertains to, concerns, relates to. Examples: A weather observation is about 'London'. A scientific observation is about 'a chemical reaction'. A bird sighting observation is about 'a specific bird species'.
observationDate: An Observation occurred on an observation date, which is the specific date or date and time when the observation was made. Also called date of observation, observed on, measurement date. Examples: A weather observation has observation date '2023-10-27'. A medical observation has observation date '2023-01-15T10:30:00Z'. An astronomical observation has observation date '2022-07-04'.
observationPeriod: An Observation spans an observation period, which is the duration over which the observation took place, expressed in ISO 8601 duration format. Also called duration of observation, measurement duration, period of study. Examples: A clinical trial observation has observation period 'P6M'. A weather station observation has observation period 'P24h'. A long-term study observation has observation period 'P5Y'. Distinct from observationDate, which is a specific point in time.
occupancy: An Accommodation specifies its occupancy, which is the allowed total number of persons (including infants) permitted to stay. Also called maximum occupancy, guest capacity, allowed persons. Examples: A hotel room has occupancy 2. An apartment has occupancy 4. A suite has occupancy 6.
occupationLocation: An Occupation is relevant to a specific occupation location, which is the administrative area (region/country) where the occupational description and requirements apply. Also called job location, work region, jurisdiction of occupation. Examples: Software Engineer occupation has occupation location 'California'. Doctor occupation has occupation location 'United Kingdom'. Teacher occupation has occupation location 'New York'.
occupationalCategory: An EducationalOccupationalProgram, JobPosting, or Occupation belongs to an occupational category, which is a classification from a recognized taxonomy like O*NET-SOC or ISCO-08. Also called job category, occupation type, employment classification. Examples: A job posting has occupational category 'Software Developers'. A medical program has occupational category 'Physicians and Surgeons'. An occupation has occupational category '25-1000' (Computer and Mathematical Occupations). Distinct from industry, which is a broader classification of the economic sector.
occupationalCredentialAwarded: A Course or EducationalOccupationalProgram grants an occupational credential awarded, which is the qualification, certificate, or diploma received upon successful completion. Also called credential earned, award upon completion, qualification granted. Examples: A coding bootcamp has occupational credential awarded 'Certificate of Completion'. A nursing program has occupational credential awarded 'Registered Nurse License'. A university course has occupational credential awarded 'Bachelor of Science'.
offerCount: An AggregateOffer includes an offer count, which is the total number of individual offers aggregated for a product. Also called number of offers, total offers, offer quantity. Examples: A product listing has offer count 10. A flight search result has offer count 50. An aggregated deal has offer count 3.
offeredBy: An Offer is offered by a specific Organization or Person, who is the entity making the offer. Also called seller, provider, made by. Examples: A product offer is offered by 'Amazon'. A service offer is offered by 'John Doe'. A job offer is offered by 'Acme Corp'. Distinct from vendor, which is a supplier.
offers: A Product, Service, Event, or other item offers a specific Demand or Offer, representing a transaction to provide that item. Also called has offer, available for purchase, provides service. Examples: A book offers 'a sale price'. A concert offers 'tickets'. A car offers 'a lease deal'. Distinct from offeredBy, which is the entity making the offer.
offersPrescriptionByMail: A HealthPlanFormulary indicates whether it offers prescription by mail, meaning prescriptions can be delivered via postal service. Also called mail-order prescriptions available, delivers prescriptions by mail, supports mail delivery of prescriptions. Examples: A health plan formulary offers prescription by mail true. A specific pharmacy offers prescription by mail false. An insurance plan offers prescription by mail true.
openingHours: A CivicStructure or LocalBusiness has opening hours, which are its general operating times specified as a weekly time range. Also called business hours, hours of operation, open times. Examples: A restaurant has opening hours 'Mo-Fr 09:00-17:00'. A museum has opening hours 'Tu-Su 10:00-18:00'. A store has opening hours 'Mo-Su 08:00-22:00'. Distinct from openingHoursSpecification, which provides structured details about opening hours.
openingHoursSpecification: A Place is associated with an opening hours specification, which provides structured details about its operating hours. Also called detailed opening times, hours specification, business hours details. Examples: A library has opening hours specification 'Monday 9am-5pm'. A park has opening hours specification 'daily sunrise to sunset'. A clinic has opening hours specification 'weekdays 8am-6pm'. Distinct from openingHours, which is a simpler text string representation.
opens: An OpeningHoursSpecification indicates when a place or service opens, specifying the start time of its operation on a given day. Also called start time, opening time, begins operation. Examples: A specification for Monday opens '09:00'. A store's daily specification opens '08:00'. A restaurant's evening specification opens '17:00'. Distinct from closes, which specifies the end time of operation.
operatingSystem: A SoftwareApplication is compatible with a specific operating system, indicating the platform it runs on. Also called supported OS, runs on, platform compatibility. Examples: A game has operating system 'Windows 10'. A mobile app has operating system 'Android'. A desktop application has operating system 'macOS'.
opponent: An ExerciseAction involves an opponent, who is the person competing against the subject of the action. Also called competitor, rival, adversary. Examples: A boxing match has opponent 'Mike Tyson'. A tennis game has opponent 'Serena Williams'. A chess match has opponent 'Magnus Carlsen'. Distinct from participant, which is a more general role.
option: A ChooseAction presents an option, which is one of the choices available for selection. Also called choice, alternative, selection. Examples: A voting action has option 'Candidate A'. A menu selection action has option 'Vegetarian'. A survey action has option 'Agree'. Distinct from object, which is the broader target of the action.
orderDate: An Order was placed on an order date, which is the specific date or date and time when the order was initiated. Also called date placed, purchase date, transaction date. Examples: A customer order has order date '2023-10-26'. An online purchase has order date '2023-10-26T14:30:00Z'. A delivery order has order date '2023-10-25'.
orderDelivery: An Order or OrderItem is associated with an order delivery, which is the specific parcel delivery related to it. Also called delivery details, shipment information, parcel associated with. Examples: A customer order has order delivery 'tracking number XYZ'. An order item has order delivery 'delivered by FedEx'. A purchase has order delivery 'scheduled for tomorrow'.
orderItemNumber: An OrderItem is identified by an order item number, which is a unique identifier for that specific item within an order. Also called item ID, line item number, order line identifier. Examples: An order item has order item number '001'. A product in an order has order item number 'A123'. The second item has order item number '2'. Distinct from orderNumber, which identifies the entire order.
orderItemStatus: An OrderItem has an order item status, which indicates its current state in the fulfillment process. Also called item status, status of order item, fulfillment status. Examples: An order item has order item status 'InTransit'. A product has order item status 'Delivered'. A backordered item has order item status 'BackOrdered'. Distinct from orderStatus, which is the status of the entire order.
orderNumber: An Order is identified by an order number, which is a unique identifier for the entire transaction. Also called transaction ID, purchase order number, reference number. Examples: A customer order has order number 'PO-12345'. An online purchase has order number 'WEB-98765'. A delivery has order number 'ORD-001'. Distinct from orderItemNumber, which identifies a specific item within an order.
orderPercentage: ShippingRateSettings specify an order percentage, which is the fraction of the total order value charged as shipping cost. Also called shipping cost percentage, shipping rate fraction, percentage of order for shipping. Examples: Shipping rate settings have order percentage 0.05. Standard shipping has order percentage 0.10. Express shipping has order percentage 0.15.
orderQuantity: An OrderItem specifies an order quantity, which is the number of units of that particular item ordered. Also called quantity ordered, item count, number of units. Examples: An order item has order quantity 2. A product in an order has order quantity 1. A bulk item has order quantity 10.
orderStatus: An Order has an order status, which indicates its current state in the fulfillment process. Also called status of order, current order state, transaction status. Examples: A customer order has order status 'OrderProcessing'. An online purchase has order status 'OrderDelivered'. A pending order has order status 'OrderProblem'. Distinct from orderItemStatus, which is the status of a specific item within an order.
orderValue: ShippingConditions are valid for a specific order value, which defines the minimum and maximum monetary amount of an order. Also called order amount range, value limit for shipping, shipping value threshold. Examples: Free shipping conditions apply to order value '$50 - $500'. Express shipping conditions apply to order value '$100 or more'. Discounted shipping conditions apply to order value '$20 - $100'.
orderedItem: An Order or OrderItem includes an ordered item, which is the specific product or service that was purchased. Also called item purchased, product bought, service acquired. Examples: An order has ordered item 'Laptop X'. An order item has ordered item 'USB Cable'. A service order has ordered item 'Consulting Service'.
organizer: An Event is managed by an organizer, who is the Organization or Person responsible for planning and executing it. Also called event planner, host, coordinator. Examples: A conference has organizer 'Tech Solutions Inc.'. A concert has organizer 'Live Nation'. A party has organizer 'Jane Doe'. Distinct from performer, who is an artist participating in the event.
originAddress: A ParcelDelivery originates from an origin address, which is the postal address of the shipper. Also called shipper's address, sender address, dispatch address. Examples: A package delivery has origin address '123 Main St, Anytown'. A shipment has origin address 'Warehouse A, City B'. A mail delivery has origin address 'Post Office, Zip 12345'. Distinct from deliveryAddress, which is the recipient's address.
originalMediaContextDescription: A MediaReview provides an original media context description, which is background information for better interpretation of decontextualized media content.
